name: PT Bukit Asam (Persero) Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bukit Asam: a price-led profit surge, a volume plan that slipped
frontmatter.summary: We keep BUY after PTBA's nine-month results and trim the target. Net profit more than trebled on a stronger selling price and almost flat cost of revenue while volumes fell, so the beat is price-led, not a volume recovery. We take the realised ratio from the print, hold the company's own delivery plan, re-derive the cost split off the lower strip ratio, and flag a third-quarter cash-conversion swing. The dividend anchor stays our caution.
thesis: The nine-month surge is a price-and-cost story, not a volume recovery: profit more than trebled on a higher average selling price and almost flat cost of revenue while sales and production both fell.
We take this year's volume at the nine-month delivery and then hold the company's own plan rather than import a second downward judgment; the long-run capacity and the reserve base are unchanged.

The realised ratio is now the one the nine-month print measures, not a haircut; it applies to a benchmark above the level it was measured on, and the compression unwinds to the last-actual calibration from the third forecast year.

The life-of-asset DCF at the coal deck's through-cycle path still values the equity well above the price, so the rating stands; the target sits above our own base scenario and the bull carries a large part of it.

Cash conversion flatters the nine months: the first half generated more operating cash than the full nine months, so the third quarter absorbed cash while profit rose — we flag the swing and do not call the print clean.
The dividend-capacity anchor sits well below the DCF and is our honest caution: it capitalises near-term earnings and the payout, not the reserve life.

catalysts.event: Fourth-quarter delivery against the full-year sales target after a weak nine months
Decision on the share buyback under review since October 2026
2027 RKAB approval and the national production ceiling
Annual GMS and FY2026 dividend determination

blocks.text: We keep our **BUY** rating and set the twelve-month target at **Rp4,989**, an expected total return of **76.0%** from the last close of Rp3,060, after PTBA's nine-month results [S11]. The update trims the near-term path, not the through-cycle value: the life-of-asset DCF still values the equity at Rp5,136 a share [S0, S5, S6].

What the nine months changed. The print is a large earnings beat and a clear volume miss. Net profit reached IDR4,410.0bn, revenue IDR35,200.0bn and EBITDA IDR7,190.0bn, with the average selling price up 18.0% and cost of revenue almost flat at IDR27,940.0bn, while sales fell to 32.23 Mt and production to 34.41 Mt [S11]. The profit surge is price-led and cost-disciplined, not the volume recovery the company's plan assumed, and we treat it that way.

What we changed in the model. Three inputs moved, each sourced to the print. First, the delivery path: nine-month sales of 32.23 Mt leave the 49.51 Mt full-year target out of reach without a fourth quarter far above anything delivered this year, so this year takes the delivery rate at 44.00 Mt; from next year we hold the company's own plan — the release reaffirms it and reports production recovering in the third quarter — at 49.50 Mt and 49.50 Mt, the company's own plan rather than a second haircut, with the approved capacity left to the bull [S7, S11]. Second, the realised ratio: the print fixes it. The disclosed nine-month revenue of IDR35,200.0bn over 32.23 Mt of sales, against the coal deck's nine-month Newcastle average translated at the deck's rupiah, gives 0.47; the ratio interpolates to 0.50 next year and returns to the last-actual calibration of 0.52 from the third forecast year [S0, S5, S11]. Third, the cost split: we take the measured strip ratio of 5.63 — the nine-month actual of 5.59 against the company's target — and re-derive the non-mining cost per tonne so the full-year total still ties to the nine-month run-rate, with the fuel inflation of 36.0% carried by the model's fuel link [S11]. No value comes from the horizon: the engine's life-end test stops the DCF well before it, so the horizon setting changes nothing we claim [S5, S7].

We withdraw the reverse-DCF variant view this round. The engine's whole-path override does not reproduce the coal deck's long-run escalation — an identity multiplier flattens the years after the explicit forecast — so any multiplier solved against it sits off the base path; that is an engine issue, escalated to the owner, and we will restore the reverse DCF when the engine reproduces the base. Instead we compare the target with our own scenarios: it sits above the base-scenario value of Rp4,629 and below the bull of Rp8,867, and the bull contributes a little under half of the probability-weighted target [S0, S5].

The honest caution is better documented now. The realised ratio compressed as the benchmark rallied, the volume plan is running short, and the dividend-capacity anchor of Rp3,370 a share sits -34.4% against the DCF because it capitalises near-term earnings and the payout, not the reserve [S5, S6, S11]. We carry that gap in the scenarios.

Bukit Asam is one of the oldest coal enterprises in the archipelago, its Tanjung Enim pits worked
since the colonial era and nationalised after independence. Indonesian thermal coal is a seaborne
swing-supply industry: the country is among the world's largest exporters, its product is mostly
medium-calorific, and its domestic power fleet consumes a mandated share of national output at
administered prices. Calorific content, transport distance and the government reference price, not
company branding, set what a tonne earns.

PTBA is an integrated Indonesian coal company, mining open-pit thermal coal around Tanjung Enim in South Sumatra with smaller operations elsewhere, and running coal transport and port infrastructure alongside the mines [S7]. Its product slate runs from a low-calorific product to a high-calorific one, with the bulk of the blend in the medium grade, represented in our model by a calorific value of 4,600 kcal/kg [S7]. It also carries downstream, power and green-business arms and holds its producing permits as IUP Operasi Produksi, with the Tanjung Enim Air Laya block under a permit dated 2020 [S7].

Sales are split between the domestic market, which took 51.5% of nine-month volume, and exports to Bangladesh, Vietnam, India, Cambodia and Thailand [S11]. The company's advantage is integration: mine-mouth rail and two dedicated coal ports give it a lower delivered cost than a mine without its own corridor, the moat that lets a medium-calorific producer earn a margin [S7]. Its weakness is product quality and a thin per-tonne margin at trough prices.

Volume grew in the last full year, with production and purchases of 47.19 Mt and sales of 45.43 Mt, but the current year has reversed: nine-month production was 34.41 Mt and sales 32.23 Mt, both below the prior year, with transport volume down further at 27.08 Mt [S7, S11]. Management attributes the earnings growth to production recovery in the third quarter, a stronger sales mix and cost discipline, and still guides to a full-year target near fifty million tonnes [S11]. A share buyback has been under review since October 2026, with no regulatory disclosure yet; we treat it as a catalyst, not as value [S2].

Indonesia's thermal-coal industry is a large, export-led swing supplier with a policy-managed domestic market. National production fell to 790 Mt in the last full year, and the government manages supply through the annual work-and-budget plan: most of the 2026 quota was approved at an aggregate level near the prior-year run-rate after an earlier proposal to tighten it sharply [S7, S9, S10]. PTBA's own plan was approved without a volume cut, but the nine months show that permits and execution are separate constraints [S3, S11].

The domestic-market obligation requires producers to sell a fixed share of output domestically, with a standing US$70/t nominal ceiling on power-station coal in the reviewed coal deck [S0]. It binds in the base case from about FY2042E as the deck's benchmark rises through it, on the power-station part of the domestic book we model; at the full domestic share it is the bear case. The royalty regime is the other structural lever: as an IUP holder PTBA pays the progressive production royalty, banded on the government's coal reference price and higher on higher-calorific tonnage, but its actual book mixes grades and domestic and export tonnes, so the effective rate it pays is the blended one we model [S5, S6].

Competitive position. PTBA is a mid-tier national producer by volume and a top-tier holder of reserves, with a reserve base the annual report puts in the billions of tonnes across its permits [S7]. Its integration along rail and port is the moat, but the same integration makes it capital-heavy and exposes it to rail and port availability — transport volume falling faster than sales in the nine months is a reminder that the corridor itself can be the constraint [S11]. Five forces: supplier power moderate, buyer power high because the domestic fleet is mandated and price-capped, substitutes rising slowly, entry barred by permits, rivalry intense in the seaborne market [S7].

The commodity frame. The house coal deck prices Newcastle f.o.b. through a mean-reverting path, with a war-premium year folding back toward a long-run marker well below spot, and the government reference price following it down [S0]. The macro desk's rupiah view is mildly weakening, which translates dollar coal revenue into more rupiah against a rupiah cost base [S0]. Both frame the valuation; we do not re-forecast them.

Actual against forecast. The nine months delivered revenue of IDR35,200.0bn, reported EBITDA of IDR7,190.0bn and net profit of IDR4,410.0bn [S11]. Two definitions have to be separated before the print is set against the forecast. The release's EBITDA is the company's own measure and is consistent with including the associate contribution of IDR581.3bn [S11]; our model's EBITDA is an operating measure — operating profit plus depreciation and amortisation — and excludes associates, which we carry below the line. On that reading the nine-month operating EBITDA is IDR7,190.0bn less the IDR581.3bn associate share, and the full-year forecast of IDR11,156.1bn is struck on the operating basis too, so the comparison is like for like [S0, S5, S11]. Net profit bridges the same way: nine-month IDR4,410.0bn less the first half's IDR2,643.4bn leaves the third quarter's contribution, and our full-year forecast of IDR7,629.6bn implies a fourth quarter materially above that third-quarter pace, not near it [S6, S11].

The fourth-quarter step-up is arithmetic from an annual build, not a second quarterly forecast. The full-year volume is the nine months plus the prior-year fourth-quarter delivery pace; the realised ratio is the one the print measures; and the full-year benchmark embeds the deck's fourth-quarter forward price, above the nine-month average [S0, S11]. Filling the nine months from the print therefore loads that price uplift into the residual quarter, and because the cost base is held flat in real terms most of it falls through to profit. We would rather say that plainly than describe the path as flat: the base case has a fourth quarter above the third quarter, and the signpost is whether the deck's forward price is realised [S0].

The mix of the beat matters more than its size. Revenue rose on sales that fell to 32.23 Mt because the average selling price rose 18.0%, against a high-calorific benchmark that rose more; cost of revenue rose only marginally to IDR27,940.0bn as the strip ratio fell to 5.59 and the company held operating costs; and the profit line also benefited from lower finance costs of IDR136.5bn and associate income of IDR581.3bn [S11]. The lift from associates and the lower finance cost are below-the-line items the DCF does not capitalise.

The model's finance charge is above the nine-month run-rate, and that is a basis difference rather than a forecast of dearer debt. The engine applies the three-year historical cost of debt to gross debt, which now includes the low-coupon back-to-back facility secured by the export-proceeds placements, while the income earned on those placements sits outside the modelled cash balance [S6, S11]. We take no value from the gap in either direction; it is a small caution inside the target, and the nine-month net finance position is the better read of the year [S11].

Cash conversion is the flag the nine-month aggregate hides. First-half operating cash flow was IDR4,625.7bn [S6] against IDR4,440.0bn for the nine months [S11], so the third quarter absorbed operating cash while profit rose from IDR2,643.4bn in the first half to IDR4,410.0bn for the nine months [S6, S11]. That is a one-quarter working-capital and receivables swing of roughly the size of the quarter's profit. The release does not decompose it, so we do not clear the print: we cannot tell from the summary whether it is receivables, tax timing or the export-proceeds placement, so we treat it as a working-capital swing and watch it at the full-year accounts; the realised-price and royalty data do not point to a revenue-recognition issue [S6, S11].

The last full year was a thin-margin year, and the restatement still drives it: revenue of IDR42,651.7bn, EBITDA of IDR5,222.2bn after the audited depreciation and amortisation charge of IDR2,014.1bn replaces the data pack's fragment, and royalties of IDR4,322.7bn, about a tenth of coal revenue [S5]. The effective royalty rate is the one we carry into the forecast, consistent with the interim accounts and with the nine-month release's nearly flat cost of revenue [S5, S6, S11].

The balance sheet remains strong but its shape changed. At the end of September cash was IDR4,890.0bn and bank loans IDR4,210.0bn, the latter including a back-to-back facility secured by export-proceeds placements [S11]. Those placements sit in the investing outflow of IDR3,500.0bn, outside cash and equivalents [S11]; netting the placements against the loans leaves net liquid assets close to the June balance sheet, so the operating move carries no separate bridge item [S6]. The bridge is struck on the June balance sheet, and that balance sheet carries the FY2025 dividend payable of IDR1,304.8bn — the dividend declared 11 June 2026 and paid 10 July 2026 [S6]. Cash owed to shareholders is not equity value, so the bridge deducts it; net cash attributable to equity is that much lower than the market block's reading: the deduction is the dividend payable itself, IDR1,304.8bn, taken before the equity value is struck. The equity-accounted stakes are untouched at book [S6].

Forecasts. We take the delivery rate for the first forecast year and hold the company's plan thereafter, holding costs at the last actual in real terms and escalating rupiah costs with Indonesian inflation and dollar prices with US inflation, the nominal-consistent treatment the house method requires [S0]. The realised ratio keeps the 2026 compression in the first year and returns to the last-actual calibration thereafter, so the long-run value is not set by a forecast-year spike or trough [S5, S11]. Capital spending is IDR3,395.0bn against the company's budget of IDR3,640.0bn, consistent with a lower-volume year [S11].

The forecast peaks with the deck's near-term price years and reverts with the benchmark, but the terminal years are not a reserve-life perpetuity: the fixed nominal DMO ceiling clips the capped power-station tonnes from about FY2042E, so free cash flow fades before the reserve is exhausted and the life-end test stops the DCF earlier than the reserve year [S0]. There is no terminal growth rate: the DCF runs on reserves and stops when marginal value turns negative.

Why this method set. PTBA is a life-of-asset commodity producer, so the primary method is a life-of-reserve DCF at the coal deck's through-cycle prices, not a spot multiple. Valuing a cyclical on current-year earnings is the classic procyclical error; the NAV uses the deck's mean-reverting path, and the other anchors are cross-checks only. The house weighting is 60% to the life DCF, 25% to EV/EBITDA and 15% to dividend capacity [S5, S6].
Cost of capital.

The build uses the risk-free rate from the house macro deck, the mature-market equity premium and Indonesia's country risk premium, an unlevered beta from the industry regression median (0.80) re-levered for the group's small net debt, and a dollar cost of debt; the resulting weighted average cost of capital is 11.2%, applied to the reserve-life cash flows [S5, S6].
Primary method.

The DCF discounts free cash flow to the firm over the reserve life, adds the June-2026 net cash after deducting the dividend payable of IDR1,304.8bn [S6], brings in the equity-accounted investments at book, and deducts minorities. It carries no terminal value because the reserves are finite. The engine's life-end test stops the DCF at the point of maximum cumulative value. In the base case the stop is set by the fixed nominal DMO ceiling clipping the capped tonnes from about FY2042E, so the DCF does not run to the full reserve year, and the long tail of a very large reserve base is not counted when it would subtract value [S0, S7]. The life the DCF runs rests on the permits as much as on the reserve: the producing block is licensed only to the end of this decade, so every later year assumes timely IUP renewal, which is how the annual report says it maintains its reserve base [S7]. Discounting at the cost of capital, roughly three-fifths of the DCF's present value sits in the years after the flagship permit's current term ends, so renewal is the largest single assumption in the valuation, not a footnote — a reader who does not accept timely renewal should not accept most of the target [S0, S7].
Cross-checks.

The EV/EBITDA anchor values the restated earnings base at a blend of the peer median and PTBA's own five-year average, and it lands -28.4% against the primary DCF [S5, S6]. The dividend-capacity anchor capitalises the modelled distribution at the sector's yield — the anchor the market most often uses for Indonesian coal names — and it lands -34.4% against the DCF. The dividend anchor is the lower of the two and the gap has widened with this update, and we explain it rather than assert a band: it capitalises a distribution of Rp398 a share struck on earnings that carry the compressed 2026 realised ratio, while the life-of-reserve DCF runs the deck's full price path over the whole reserve life. The divergence is about where in the price cycle each method looks, not about the asset, and the house weights favour the DCF [S5, S7].

Sensitivity. We withhold the benchmark-and-rupiah grid this round. Every grid that shocks the benchmark runs through the engine's whole-path override, which flattens the deck's post-explicit escalation, so the centre cell does not reconcile with the target and we will not publish a table we cannot stand behind [S0]. The engine's volume-and-cost-intensity grid does not touch the benchmark, is clean, and its centre reproduces the base value, so the ranking below rests on a run we can defend [S0]. The rank order is unchanged: a life-of-reserve value is most sensitive to the realised price and the rupiah, and least to volume at the margin — an inventory-of-reserves business, not a growth business [S0, S5]. The one judgement the price grids do not settle is how much of the domestic book sits under the cap. We charge it to the power-station share, the bear charges it to the whole domestic book, and the FY2025 accounts identify the PLN group as the only customer above a tenth of revenue at IDR14,429.2bn [S5, S11]. A higher power share than our mid-point lowers the capped tonnage's realisation and the value — the direction the bear already prices — so the base is bracketed by the scenario table rather than by a second grid.

What the price implies. We do not publish a reverse-DCF multiplier this round, for the same engine reason: a multiplier solved on the flattened path is not on the base path [S0]. The directional reading does not depend on the grid. The target sits above the base-scenario value of Rp4,629 and below the bull of Rp8,867, and the market price of Rp3,060 sits between the bear-scenario value of Rp1,834 and the base, much closer to the bear: the market is assigning materially more weight to the downside state than the quarter we carry, and the gap to our base is a probability disagreement rather than a different view of the reserve value [S5, S6]. Calibration note: re-pricing the last actual year at its own benchmark, volume, realised ratio and rupiah reproduces the LK's EBITDA to within a couple of per cent, with the residual carried by the cost split, which is struck on the nine-month run-rate and the current fuel basis; the engine's headline gap is wider because it prices FY2025A's volume and benchmark at the FY2026E realised ratio and rupiah [S5, S11].
Downside risks, with our view of likelihood and impact.

items: **Commodity price (high likelihood, high impact).** The benchmark reverting through the deck's
long-run marker below spot is the base case, and a deeper oversupply — Chinese and Indian restarts,
relaxed Indonesian supply discipline — takes realised prices below our path. The per-tonne margin is
thin at trough prices, so small price moves are large earnings moves [S0].
**Realisation compression (high likelihood, medium impact).** The nine-month record shows the
medium-calorific book captured much less of the benchmark rally than the high-calorific index, so
the compression we now carry could persist beyond the next year rather than unwind [S11].
**Volume execution (high likelihood, high impact).** Nine-month sales ran well below the plan and
transport volumes fell faster, so the recovery we assume is a forecast, not a delivered fact; a
repeat of the first nine months removes the second-half volume the plan needs [S11].
**Domestic policy and quota (medium likelihood, high impact).** A tightened RKAB ceiling, or a
domestic-market obligation applied at a lower price, would cut volume or realisation. PTBA's own
RKAB was approved without a cut, but national policy has swung before [S9, S10].
**Currency (medium likelihood, medium impact).** A sharply stronger rupiah compresses the dollar
revenue translated into rupiah while the cost base stays in rupiah; the reverse is the tailwind in
our forecast [S0].
**Cost inflation (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Fuel prices rose 36.0% in the nine
months and offset the lower strip ratio; a sustained fuel price or a higher strip ratio as pits
deepen would raise cash cost per tonne [S11].
**Working capital (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The third quarter absorbed operating cash
while profit rose; a repeat would turn the earnings beat into a receivables story and cut the
dividend the capacity anchor capitalises [S6, S11].
**Governance and related parties (low likelihood, medium impact).** A state-controlled issuer with a
majority related-party revenue book carries the modal Indonesian value-destruction risk; the flows
are disclosed and priced off third-party terms, but they are large [S5, S7].

blocks.text: Scenarios.

Bear: the state takes a larger share of a state-owned producer — a work-and-budget cut toward the lower national ceiling the government proposed before approving the higher one, or a tighter domestic-market obligation at the capped power price — while the benchmark rolls back through the deck's long-run marker and the medium-calorific book keeps the realised price a fifth weaker on the company's own ratio, so the whole price path, escalation included, moves down with it. Volume is cut about five million tonnes below the base, the price cap is charged to the whole domestic book rather than the power-station share — the policy upper bound — and the payout falls to the FY2025 trough ratio as earnings fall. The volume risk is visible in the actuals: the nine months ran below the plan, so the bear is a continuation of what has been delivered, not a hypothesis [S9, S10, S11]. Bull: a sustained war-premium holds the benchmark above the long-run marker and the realised price is shocked a fifth above the base path — the mirror of the bear's cut, and a scenario boundary rather than a claim that the ratio returns to an observed level, because the three published years do not bound a tail — as the medium-calorific spread narrows and the export share rises [S5, S11]. The price cap stays at the base power-station share, and the payout returns to the boom-year ratio PTBA's own record demonstrates. Volume adds only half a million tonnes because the base already runs at the company's plan level from the third year, so the add reaches the approved capacity exactly — a larger bull would be above the RKAB ceiling — and the upside is carried on realised price and payout, not on above-capacity tonnes [S7, S11]. Both tails shock the same four drivers — realised price, volume, the capped domestic share and payout — with mirrored price and payout moves and two sourced asymmetries: the capacity cap on the bull's volume and the policy cap on the bear's domestic share.

The target is above our own base scenario. At the house probabilities the base contributes the largest single share, the bull a little under half on its quarter weight, and the bear the remainder; the bull carries Rp8,867 against the base of Rp4,629, so the rating leans on a state in which the realised ratio and the payout recover while the price holds [S5, S8]. We consider that state as likely as the bear, which is why the target sits above the base — it is a probability-weighted number, not a base-case number: the target sits below the primary DCF of Rp5,136 and below the bull.

The optionality the base case does not pay for. The bull now carries the higher payout, which is how we quantify the buyback and distribution optionality rather than asserting it: a payout back at the boom-year ratio flows straight into the dividend-capacity anchor and is worth the bull's Rp8,867 against the base [S7, S8]. Beyond the reserve base we value, the annual report carries a resource inventory roughly twice the proved-and-probable reserve, including a large un-developed block at Banko Tengah; converting even part of it extends the modelled life rather than changing near-term cash flows, so we treat it as upside prose, not value [S7].

Signposts that would change our view: the realised ratio recovering while the benchmark rolls over; a formal buyback or higher dividend policy; an RKAB cut applied to PTBA itself; a rupiah break either way; delivered volume close to the full-year plan; and any sign of a lower domestic price [S2, S8, S10, S11].

Ownership and control. PTBA is state-controlled: the government holds the special Dwiwarna share and the MIND ID mining holding owns 65.9% of the register, with the public holding the balance and a small treasury position [S7]. Strategy follows the holding's direction, and major corporate actions need board and shareholder approval — the structure that governs the buyback now under review [S2, S7].

Related parties. Related-party revenue is large because state entities are related parties under the Indonesian accounting standards; the audited note puts coal revenue from related parties at a majority of coal sales in the last actual year [S5]. This is a disclosure-quality point rather than a red flag — the flows are to the domestic power fleet and other state buyers — but we do not take arm's length on trust, because the same state sets both the domestic price ceiling and the reference price that bands the royalty. The test we apply is whether the blended realised price the company actually achieves sits below the government reference price for its calorific band: the nine-month record shows the realised price below the contemporaneous benchmark and the royalty charged at the blended schedule rate, which is what arm's-length state pricing under the domestic-market rules looks like [S5, S6, S11]. The company states it has no material conflict-of-interest transactions [S7]. The reclamation and mine-closure obligation is a balance-sheet provision and is reflected in the accounts; it is not an incremental DCF charge because the life-end test truncates the model ahead of reserve exhaustion [S5, S6].

Audit and reporting. The last full year's consolidated statements carry an unmodified opinion from KAP Purwantono, Susanti dan Surja, a member firm of Ernst & Young Global, with no special GMS status, going-concern notation or qualification [S5]. The nine-month release is an unaudited press summary, so we weight the audited annual figures and expect the usual fourth-quarter true-ups [S11].

Dividends. The stated policy is to distribute at least a set share of net profit under the IPO prospectus unless the GMS decides otherwise, with a long record of paying above that floor [S7]. The FY2025 book dividend was approved at the June-2026 annual GMS at IDR1,310.0bn, a payout well above the policy floor but below the boom-year payouts [S7, S8]. Our modelled payout sits between the floor and that record, and the stronger 2026 earnings lift the modelled distribution to Rp398 a share [S8, S11].

ESG exposures. PTBA's material issues are land and biodiversity around the Tanjung Enim and Kalimantan pits, mine-closure and reclamation liabilities, water and tailings management, and the transition risk of a thermal-coal franchise. It carries a reclamation and mine-closure provision and reports sustainability and climate disclosures alongside the annual report, and it is a large regional employer running community programmes [S5, S7]. The transition is the structural risk: a net-zero path and the grid's renewables build eventually shrink the domestic thermal market, and the reserve life we value reaches well into that horizon.
Dated catalysts are in the frontmatter: fourth-quarter delivery against target, a buyback decision, the annual GMS that sets the FY2026 dividend, and the 2027 work-and-budget plan [S2, S8, S10, S11].

Between updates we monitor a short list. First, the price side: the Newcastle benchmark and the government reference price off the coal deck, spot against the deck's path, and the rupiah off the macro deck [S0]. Second, the company's own delivery: quarterly volumes and realised price against the plan and against the ratio we have calibrated, the stripping ratio and the cash cost per tonne against the last actual, and the transport volumes on the Tanjung Enim corridor [S11]. Third, the cash side: the full-year bridge from operating cash flow to profit, after the third-quarter swing [S6, S11]. Fourth, the policy side: the RKAB decision, any change to the domestic-market obligation or the price ceiling, and any royalty-order change [S3, S5, S9, S10].

The number that would move our rating most is the realised price-to-benchmark ratio recovering while the benchmark rolls over: that is the bull case, it is not in the base case, and we would re-underwrite on the first report of it [S5, S7]. The second is a formal buyback or a higher dividend policy, which would lift the dividend-capacity anchor that sits below the DCF [S2, S8].

bear.narrative: Newcastle rolls back through the deck's long-run floor as Chinese and Indian mine restarts and relaxed Indonesian RKAB discipline turn the 2025-26 war-premium tightness into oversupply, and the state takes a larger share of a state-owned producer: an RKAB cut toward the ~600 Mt national level the government proposed before approving ~720 Mt, or a tighter DMO at the capped power price, cuts PTBA's volume by about a tenth while its medium-CV, domestic-heavy blend keeps the realised-to-benchmark ratio compressed as the benchmark falls. The realised price is shocked on the company ratio (0.8x) rather than on the benchmark deck, so the whole price path, including its long-run escalation, moves together. The DMO ceiling is tightened to the whole domestic book (0.54 of volume, the upper bound), so the fixed nominal cap bites earlier and truncates the modelled life, and the dividend steps down to the FY2025 trough payout as earnings fall.

bull.narrative: A sustained war-premium in seaborne thermal coal and Chinese import curbs keep Newcastle above the deck's long-run marker, and the realised price is shocked a fifth above the base path — the mirror of the bear's cut, which takes the realised-to-benchmark ratio above the FY2025A calibration rather than toward it. That is a scenario boundary, not a forecast of an observed ratio: the three published years (FY2023-25) do not bound a tail, and the ratio can rise without any observed level being contradicted if the medium-CV spread narrows and the export share keeps rising. Production returns to the company's 49.5 Mt plan and the 50 Mt capacity, which caps the volume upside, and the extra dollars convert into cash against a rupiah cost base that does not move with them. The DMO ceiling stays at the base share, royalty stays flat at the LK's effective rate in both tails (no scenario switches to the banded schedule), and the higher distribution PTBA's record demonstrates is paid as the payout returns to its FY2023-24 level. Both tails shock the same four drivers — realised price, volume, capped domestic share and payout — with mirrored price, volume and payout moves; the volume and cap asymmetries are the capacity limit and the downside-only policy cap, justified in qc_justifications.

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: DATE 2026-10-29 revision. FY2026E is the 9M-2026 delivery rolled to a full year: sales ran 32.23 Mt in the nine months to September (F36, S11) and hitting the 49.51 Mt target (F42) would need a Q4 of 17.28 Mt — 47% above Q4-2025's 11.73 Mt (FY2025 45.43 Mt, F1, less 33.70 Mt in 9M 2025, S11). Q4 at the prior-year pace gives about 44 Mt, so FY2026E is 44.0 Mt. From FY2027E we hold the company's own plan rather than a judgment glide: the 9M release reaffirms production of 49.55 Mt and sales of 49.51 Mt (F42, S11) and reports production recovering in Q3, so FY2027E is 49.5 Mt, the last sourced forward level, and FY2028E onward holds 49.5 Mt — the company's own plan, not a haircut, and below the 50 Mt RKAB-approved capacity (S3, S11) only because the plan is the sourced level. The bull adds half a million tonnes to reach the approved capacity; a larger volume would be above the RKAB ceiling. The 9M shortfall is a 2026 execution miss, not evidence of a permanently lower capability: production fell 4.1% to 34.41 Mt (F37) while the plan was reaffirmed (F42), and the earlier plan basis was management's optimistic delivery guidance (S4). No default haircut is carried into 2027-28.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: DATE 2026-10-29 revision. FY2026E 0.471 is the ratio the 9M-2026 print produces, not a haircut. Numerator: coal revenue is not disclosed for the nine months, so the measurement uses the disclosed 9M revenue of Rp35.20trn (F35, S11) on 32.23 Mt of sales (F36), about Rp1,092,000/t; total revenue includes the small non-coal book (H1 other-activity revenue is Rp357.6bn on F19 less F26), which overstates the coal ASP by about 1.5%, so the true coal ratio sits a shade below 0.471 — still above the 0.4635 previously carried. Denominator: the coal deck's 2026 Newcastle average of about US$131.9/t (Q1 122.3, Q2 135.4, Q3 138.1), translated at the deck's FY2026E rupiah of 17,570: 1,092,000 / (131.9 x 17,570) = 0.471. The release's ASP +18% against Newcastle +25% and ICI-3 +26% (F51, S11) confirms that the medium-CV, 51.5%-domestic book (F50, F15) captured less than the high-CV benchmark. FY2026E applies the ratio to the full-year benchmark of US$137.0, which is 3.8% above the nine-month average because it embeds the Q4 forward curve (149-153, coal deck); at a stable ratio that reproduces the full-year ASP, and no Q4 lag is added. Because the model is annual, filling the nine months from the print loads that 3.8% full-year price uplift into the residual fourth quarter, which is why the implied Q4 profit sits above the third quarter's run-rate — disclosed in report section 3 and consistent with the annual build, not a separate quarterly forecast. FY2027E 0.497 interpolates between the 9M observation and the FY2025A calibration 0.5175 at the deck's lower FY2027E benchmark of US$118.0; from FY2028E the model holds the FY2025A calibration (realised Rp922,499/t on 45.43 Mt over the FY2025A Newcastle average of US$108.4/t), the last full actual year, to lt, as the desk rule requires: the last full actual year sets the long-run ratio, and the 2026 compression is the war-premium year unwinding. The drift FY2026E -> lt is +9.9%, below the engine's 10% ratio threshold, so the engine raises no drift flag and no separate justification key is needed.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: DATE 2026-10-29 revision (QC Q2). 0.27 is half the domestic upper bound, not the upper bound itself: the deck's US$70/t ceiling is a nominal power-station price (d.coal.dmo_cap, lt 70, no escalation) and it is charged only to the power-station part of the book, not to every domestic tonne. Domestic sales were 54% of FY2025 volume (S7 p.65) and 51.5% in 9M-2026 (F50, S11), and the annual report says domestic supply goes "particularly to power plants" (S7) without publishing the split, so the base charges the cap to about half the domestic book (power), and the BEAR doubles it to 0.54 — all domestic tonnes at the capped power price — while the BULL holds the base share. This is a stated bound-splitting judgement between two no-disclosure endpoints, not a disclosed figure. The realised ratio (calibrated on the FY2025A actual, when the US$70 cap did not bind) already embeds today's domestic power pricing. Not inert: the engine's own run at 0.54 showed the cap biting from FY2042E and truncating the DCF at FY2051E instead of the reserve year.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: DATE 2026-10-29 revision. 5.63x is the company's own 2026 target and the 9M-2026 run-rate: the strip ratio fell from 5.98x to 5.59x in the nine months, against a 5.63x full-year target (F41/F42, S11), not the FY2025A actual of 6.06x (F16). It is the intensity factor that multiplies cost_per_bcm; the cost split is re-derived below so the FY2026E total still ties to the 9M run-rate, with the lower strip intensity offset inside other_cost_unit and the fuel link (fuel prices +36% yoy, F54/S11). No grade or mine-plan drift is asserted.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: IDR 50,000/bcm (about US$3.0/bcm at the FY2025A rate), the sector norm for Indonesian open-pit overburden removal by contractors — the same US$3.0/bcm the COAL peer set uses. PTBA does not disclose a per-bcm rate, so the split between this and other_cost_unit is a proxy chosen so that strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm plus other_cost_unit lands the FY2025A LK cash cost. Held flat in nominal terms; the engine grows it at the IDR long-run inflation scalar after FY2030E.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — PTBA does not break out fuel; sector norm retained

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: IDR 374,738/t: the balancing item that brings total cash cost to the LK-calibrated level, re-derived for the 5.63x strip ratio. Derivation unchanged: FY2025A cost of revenues Rp36,394,624m (S5 p.128) less royalties to government Rp4,322,659m (F11) less the D&A charged inside cost of revenues (depreciation Rp1,575,007m + amortisation Rp135,726m = Rp1,710,733m, S5 p.128) = Rp30,361,232m of group cash operating cost; the cost of the Rp742,638m of other-activity revenue (F13, S5 Catatan 26) is charged separately on the other_cogs line at Rp668,374m (742,638 x (1 - other_margin)), so the coal cash cost is 30,361,232 - 668,374 = Rp29,692,858m; divided by 45.43 Mt (F1) = Rp653,597/t. The strip component at 5.63x and IDR50,000/bcm is Rp281,500/t, and the fuel uplift at the FY2026E brent of 96.0 (30% fuel share, about +41% against FY2025A) is roughly Rp34,600/t, so other_cost_unit = 690,835 - 281,500 - 34,600 = about Rp374,738/t: the FY2026E total stays at the 9M run-rate while the strip decomposition follows the actual. It carries PTBA's heavy haulage and rail/port cost — the H1-2026 LK shows coal transportation services of Rp3,998,563m as the second-largest cash line inside cost of revenues, behind mining services of Rp5,737,978m (S6 Catatan 27a). Held flat in nominal terms, then grown at IDR inflation.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat-regime fallback; not used under tier mode)
assumptions.basis: The LK's effective royalty rate, charged flat on coal revenue. FY2025A: royalties to government Rp4,322,659m (F11, S5 p.128) on coal revenue Rp41,909,086m (F13, S5 p.127) = 10.31%; FY2024A 9.69% (Rp4,077,822m / Rp42,084,008m). The H1-2026 interim confirms it again: Rp2,209,879m of royalties (S6 Catatan 27a) on Rp21,672,370m of coal revenue (S6 Catatan 26) = 10.20%. The owner directive (MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE) requires the LK's effective rate in the base case, so the model is flat here rather than applying the top IUP band to every tonne: PTBA sells 54% of its volume domestically (S7 p.65) off a 2,800-6,100 GAR slate (F15), so its book mixes the low and mid tranches of the PP 19/2025 schedule and the blended paid rate is the most-likely one. All three scenarios keep this flat effective rate: none switches royalty_mode or the schedule, so the bull is not credited with the banded schedule — at its higher realised price the top band would tax coal revenue above the flat rate, so if the flat rate biases the bull at all it flatters it.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A other revenue of Rp742,638m = total revenue Rp42,651,724m less coal revenue Rp41,909,086m (F13, S5) — trading, transport, palm and services across PTBA's subsidiaries (S7). Held flat in nominal terms and escalated at IDR inflation beyond FY2030E.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default constant

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: IDR 44,334/t = the LK's own consolidated depreciation AND amortisation of Rp2,014,102m in FY2025 (F7, S5 p.159, segment additional disclosures) divided by 45.43 Mt (F1). This is the RESTATEMENT the desk rule demands: the data pack's D&A of Rp300,136m is only ~15% of the real charge, because the IDX direct cash-flow presentation carries no D&A line and the pack picked up a fragment. The segment note is the anchor because PTBA's mine-property depletion is amortised on a unit-of-production basis inside cost of revenues and is not in the income-statement depreciation line. Held flat in real terms, then escalated at IDR inflation.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: IDR 77,159/t = FY2025A capital expenditure of Rp3,505,367m (F9, S5 p.20 cash-flow statement, "perolehan aset tetap dan tanaman produktif") divided by 45.43 Mt (F1). FY2025 was an investment peak — FY2024 capex was Rp1,231,886m (F10), about IDR 28,700/t on that year's volume — because the Tanjung Enim-Kramasan coal-transport project and the downstream/power build ran through the year (S7). We use the last actual, as the rule requires, and flag that it is the top of the recent range in §3 and the sensitivity table; no drifts are asserted.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — the growth project spend is carried inside capex_unit (FY2025A peak) rather than added again here

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue))

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt)) — FY2025A was 21.6% (tax Rp813,973m on pbt Rp3,773,209m, S5)

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — no disclosed borrowing plan; PTBA is close to net cash

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items (recurring associate income)
assumptions.basis: DATE 2026-10-29 revision (QC Q3). Carries the recurring share of associates and joint ventures so forecast profit, DPS and the dividend anchor are on a consolidated basis: 9M-2026 associate income was Rp581.31bn, +75% yoy (F48, S11), so the full-year run-rate is about Rp775bn (581.31 x 4/3). The stakes are added at book in the bridge and the DCF does not capitalise this below-the-line income, so there is no double count; it enters pbt and therefore np and the dividend. Held flat in nominal terms, then escalated at IDR inflation. One-off items are not included.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Held at 0.60 against a realised record that bracketed it: the FY2025 book dividend of Rp1.31trn / Rp114.50 per share (F20, S8) is 45% of FY2025 net profit — the trough of the cycle, when earnings were lowest and the transport build was still to be funded — while the FY2023 and FY2024 payouts ran at roughly three-quarters of earnings (S7 p.31, the annual report's dividend history). The stated policy floor is 30% of net profit unless the GMS decides otherwise (S7 p.242). 0.60 is not the cautious pick: it sits above both the policy floor and the most recent (low-year) print and below the boom-year record, and it is the mid-point the company's own record supports for a normal year while a heavy capex programme still runs; management said any buyback decision would consider working-capital needs (S2), which argues against assuming the full boom-year ratio. It carries only the 0.15 div_yield weight and no weight in the primary DCF.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — single-class share count, no issue planned; a buyback is under review but not executed (S2)

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Zero: the DCF is a finite life-of-reserve value at the deck's long-run price and the engine's reserves line truncates production at the 2,883 Mt reserve base (F5) before the 70-year horizon, and the life-end test stops the cash flows earlier still (FY2050E), so no perpetuity growth is added — the COAL peer convention (GEMS, BYAN).

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at 6.44497%, the LK's cash SG&A net of other income, struck on the restated total revenue so the line carries the same basis as history. The LK's own operating expenses (Beban usaha) are Rp3,152,672m in FY2025A (S5 p.159 segment note, G&A Rp2,340,071m plus selling Rp812,601m); the depreciation booked inside them (Rp125,421m in G&A plus Rp174,715m in selling = Rp300,136m, S5 Notes 27b/27c p.11398/11419) is stripped because the model charges the FULL D&A separately on the da line, and the other income – net of Rp103,645m (S5 p.17) is deducted so the ratio reproduces the LK's operating profit. That leaves Rp2,748,891m of cash SG&A over revenue Rp42,651,724m (F24). Sourced to the LK, NOT to the data pack's opex, which is a plug (gross profit less the pack's understated EBIT) and overstates the line by about Rp157bn. Broadly proportional to revenue (selling costs include the volume-linked haulage/marketing charges), so held flat.

challenges.challenge: An identity multiplier on the coal deck is not a no-op. Re-running the model with d.coal.newc x1.0 gives a benchmark flat at US$107.1 from FY2031E all the way to FY2095E (instead of the deck's escalating 109.24 ... 387.97), a life DCF of 3,554 a share against the base 5,112, and a life-end of FY2037E against FY2050E. The cause is _apply_overrides writing every forecast label back into the deck values, so each later year re-derives the lt escalation from the previous explicit year and the escalation never compounds; an identity shock must reproduce the base and does not. Consequently every run that shocks d.coal.newc sits on a different price path from the base: the published newc/USD sensitivity grid's centre cell is 3,488 against the base 4,619 (the clean strip/volume grid centres on 4,619, confirming the control), and that grid is non-monotonic (2,264 at x0.8, 1,934 at x0.9). The bull DCF is 11,723 on the flattened path against 13,786 on the true path, so at the 70% DCF weight the bull target is understated by roughly 1,400 a share and the 5,181 weighted target by roughly 350 (about 7%). The reverse-DCF factor 0.986 is solved against a flat-path DCF of 3,554; on the true escalating path the 3,280 price implies a multiplier near 0.935 (about US$110 at FY2027E and US$98 at the lt marker), not 0.986/US$116.4. The report's central "market prices the house long-run view a shade below parity" and the attribution of the discount to the balance sheet and reserves are therefore built on the wrong base.
challenges.answer: Accepted as an engine defect, not a modelling choice, and reproduced: an identity multiplier on d.coal.newc returns a flat US$107.1 path instead of the deck's escalating 109.24 to 387.97, so every earlier newc-shocked run — both tails, both grids, the reverse DCF — sat off the base path. scripts/ is not editable by the analyst, so the fix is escalated to the engine owner. In the meantime: the reverse-DCF variant view, the "a shade below parity" attribution and the newc/USD grid are withdrawn from §4 and the summary; reverse-DCF output is excluded from the target and from qc_justifications.extreme_call; the price shock is carried on a.realisation, which scales every year of the same deck path including the lt-escalated years (justified in qc_justifications.scenario.price_driver); and both scenarios, the price-implies paragraph and the sensitivity paragraph are rewritten on that basis. The reverse DCF and grid will be restored when an identity shock reproduces the base.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E realisation of 0.4635 is not reproducible from the derivation given. The basis divides 9M revenue of Rp35.20trn on 32.23 Mt (about Rp1.092m/t) by the nine-month Newcastle average of about US$131.9/t at the deck's FY2026E rupiah of 17,570, which gives about 0.471, not 0.4635. The release's ASP +18% against Newcastle +25% and ICI-3 +26% (S11) is consistent with a ratio near 0.47-0.49 depending on the 9M-2025 base, not a 10% compression. The ratio is then applied to the full-year benchmark of 137.0, which is above the 131.9 it was measured against, with no Q4 price-lag bridge. The 1.5-2% gap is an unsourced haircut on the largest revenue driver, carried into every modelled tonne of FY2026E.
challenges.answer: Accepted; the haircut is removed. FY2026E is set to 0.471, the ratio the stated inputs produce, with the derivation now written out: numerator Rp1,092,000/t (9M revenue Rp35.20trn over 32.23 Mt of sales), denominator US$131.9/t (the deck's 2026 Newcastle average: Q1 122.3, Q2 135.4, Q3 138.1) at the deck's FY2026E rupiah of 17,570, i.e. 1,092,000 / (131.9 x 17,570) = 0.471; the 1.5% non-coal revenue overstatement is noted. The full-year benchmark of 137.0 is applied at a stable ratio with no Q4 lag claimed, because 137.0 embeds the deck's Q4 forward curve and is 3.8% above the nine-month average, so the ratio on a higher full-year price reproduces the full-year ASP rather than lagging it. FY2027E 0.497 interpolates to the FY2025A calibration 0.5175, held from FY2028E to lt. The drift gate does not fire on realisation: the 0.471 to 0.5175 path is +9.9%, under the engine's 10% ratio threshold, so no qc_justifications.drift.realisation key exists or is needed (QC Q5 corrects the earlier wording, which said one was added).

challenges.challenge: The report states "operating cash flow of Rp4.44trn was in line with reported profit, so there is no accruals flag". That is an H1 artifact: H1-2026 operating cash flow was Rp4,625.730bn (S6 p.13) against Rp4,440bn for the nine months (S11), so Q3 standalone operating cash flow was about negative Rp186bn while Q3 net profit was about Rp1,767bn (9M Rp4,410bn less H1 Rp2,643.357bn). That is a one-quarter accrual divergence of roughly Rp1.95trn, in receivables or working capital, and it is exactly the earnings-quality test the report says it passed. The 9M aggregate hides it because H1 was strongly cash-generative.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The "no accruals flag" sentence is removed. The Q3 bridge is now disclosed as the earnings-quality flag: H1-2026 operating cash flow of Rp4,625.730bn (F52, S6 p.13) against Rp4,440bn for the nine months (F46, S11), so Q3 standalone operating cash flow was negative, while Q3 net profit was about Rp1,767bn (9M Rp4,410bn F34 less H1 Rp2,643.357bn F53) — a one-quarter working-capital and receivables swing of roughly the quarter's profit. The press release does not decompose the swing, so the report says so, treats it as a working-capital and export-proceeds placement effect rather than asserting a cause, notes that the realised-price and royalty data show nothing accrual-like on revenue, and adds a working-capital risk bullet and a full-year cash-bridge monitoring line. The Q3 figures are derived from the H1 and 9M filings by placeholder arithmetic in prose; no new fact is typed.

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative names a tightened RKAB ceiling, a domestic-market obligation at a lower price and a rupiah break, but the bear shocks contain none of them: only newc x0.8, volume x0.95, realisation x0.9 and other_cost_unit +30,000. A state-controlled producer selling 51.5% domestically (16.62 Mt of 32.23 Mt, S11) faces a policy shock that hits volume and realisation together; a rupiah appreciation, which the report itself lists as a medium-likelihood risk, would compress IDR revenue while costs stay in rupiah and is in no scenario. The probability-weighted target therefore has no state in which either named policy or currency risk occurs.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The bear now numerically carries the policy state its narrative names: a.realisation x0.8 (the whole realised price path, escalation included), a.volume -5.0 Mt (the 9M shortfall and the RKAB/DMO cut the release and policy news describe), a.capped_share x2.0 (the whole domestic book at the capped power price, the upper bound) and a.payout x0.75 (the FY2025 trough ratio), with the narrative naming the ~600 Mt national ceiling and a tighter DMO at the capped power price (QC Q2 later fixed the base cap at the power-station share and moved the full domestic bound into this bear state). FX is not separately shocked: the engine's deck override flattens the macro path the same way it flattens the coal path (C1), so an FX-shocked state would sit off the base path; the rupiah remains a stated medium-likelihood risk and a weekly monitored variable instead, and the bear's realisation cut already abstracts the currency effect at the revenue line. Both tails now shock the same four drivers, so the probability-weighted target has a state in which policy occurs.

challenges.challenge: FY2027E 47.0 Mt and FY2028E 49.0 Mt are below the company's own 2026 sales plan of 49.51 Mt (F42, S11) and below the 50 Mt RKAB-approved capacity the model calls the long-run level. The basis calls 47.0 "halfway between the 44 Mt delivery and the 49.5 Mt plan" - a judgment, not a source. The 9M miss sources the FY2026E cut, not a two-year recovery that stays below the plan the company reaffirmed for 2026.
challenges.answer: Accepted. FY2027E is raised to 49.5 Mt and FY2028E to lt to 49.5 Mt — the company's own reaffirmed plan (production 49.55 Mt, sales 49.51 Mt, F42/S11), which the 9M release restates, rather than a judgment glide halfway between delivery and plan. The basis now says the plan is the sourced level and the 50 Mt RKAB capacity is left to the bull; the 9M miss is treated as a 2026 execution miss supported by production down 4.1% (F37) with the plan reaffirmed (F42), and no default haircut is carried into 2027-28. The FY2026E 44.0 Mt remains the delivery rate, sourced to the 9M actual and the prior-year Q4 pace.

challenges.challenge: The report's own optionality - resources of 5,713 Mt against 2,883 Mt reserves including Banko Tengah (F5, S7 p.104), the buyback under review since October 2026 (S2), and a higher payout - is in prose only. The 25%-weighted bull is a price/volume/realisation/cost bull and none of these is in any scenario or sensitivity row; the base case "does not pay for" them by construction. The report therefore asserts upside it never quantifies, and the target cannot be tested against it.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The bull now carries a payout sensitivity, a.payout x1.25 back toward the FY2023-24 boom-year ratio (S7 dividend history), which flows into the dividend-capacity anchor and is quantified in the table: the bull scenario value is now the single number that shows what the higher distribution (and, indirectly, the buyback optionality) is worth. The buyback itself stays a catalyst, not value, because it is still undisclosed (S2), and reserve conversion remains upside prose rather than a valued line: it extends the modelled life, which the life-end test truncates anyway. The report states which optionality is quantified and which is not.

challenges.challenge: The bull contributes as much to the target as the base: 0.25 x 9,221.55 = 2,305 of the 5,180.96 target (44.5%), against 0.50 x 4,619.32 = 2,310 (44.6%) from the base and 565.92 (10.9%) from the bear. The target sits above both its own base scenario (4,619) and the primary DCF (5,112). The bull's volume shock is x1.05, i.e. 52.5 Mt at the FY2029E volume of 50 Mt - above the RKAB-approved capacity and the rail/port system the report says was built for 50 Mt. An unsourced above-capacity volume assumption carries 44% of the target.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Bull volume is now +0.5 Mt on a base that holds 49.5 Mt from FY2028E, so the bull reaches 50 Mt — the RKAB-approved capacity exactly — instead of 52.5 Mt; the add is sourced by the capacity cap, and the justification is rewritten (once 52.5 Mt was unsourced and above both the capacity and the 25 Mt/yr corridor). The target exceeding the base scenario is now stated explicitly in §4 and §5: the target is a probability-weighted number, the bull contributes a little under half on its quarter weight, and the base contributes the largest single share. The report also states that the target sits below the primary DCF and below the bull, so the reader can see how much of the target the tail carries.

On the base path the price sits far below the DCF value of the reserve life; the two cross-check anchors (EV/EBITDA and dividend capacity) sit below the DCF because they capitalise near-term earnings and the payout, which is the honest caution carried in the bear case and the cross-check discussion.
